articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.content: Pair clashed at PMQs over a video shot outside No 10 by TikToker Max Balegde Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration. Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov. Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters. It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity. Continue reading...

articles.author: Emma Brockes
articles.content: For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape. To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett , was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”. Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Nesrine Malik, in East Jerusalem
articles.content: Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem. Continue reading...

articles.content: From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective power • Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.content: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life. Touring Europe until 2 May Continue reading...

The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life. Touring Europe until 2 May Continue reading...

articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.content: Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak , which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating . Continue reading...

articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull , Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal ) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford . This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.content: From a V-neck sweater worn back-to-front to a perfectly framed collarbone – here’s the secret to low-stakes sex appeal I’m not sure when it started being not chic to want to look sexy, but it’s definitely a thing and it bothers me as it doesn’t feel truthful to the human experience, if that’s not a lot for the first sentence of a fashion column. Our wardrobes have become shrines to good taste. Well-cut coats and quality knitwear, elegant flat shoes and crisp white shirts. These clothes are excellent at communicating that you have read the briefing notes for the meeting and have some Booker prize chat. They are less good at suggesting you might be up for dancing on a table later. Why do we have to choose? Clothes have always been partly about how they make us feel physically. We accept that an outfit can make you feel powerful, cool, smart. Why shouldn’t it also make you feel hot and fun? Continue reading...

articles.content: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity to see just how fast I could run; the 100-metre track at school never drew out of me what running for my life did. Nadia didn’t care about any of that, but she humoured me anyway. Continue reading...

articles.content: Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro , an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation. “Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Peter Bradshaw
articles.content: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sid Lowe in Madrid
articles.content: Englishman hailed by teammates and manager Mourinho after coming on to completely change Champions League game against PSV Eindhoven “It was one of those moments when you’re just: ‘Wow.’” Bernardo Silva had a good view of Jude Bellingham scoring the goal, the golazo , that put Real Madrid into the lead and the Bernabéu on its feet, shock giving way to song, naa, naa, naa, na-na-na-naa, na-na-na-naa ringing round again. “I have no idea what I did,” the Englishman said afterwards. What he did was turn all Le Tissier. Lifting the ball with his left, raising it with his right, twisting and not letting it drop, he sent it arching from the outside of his boot into the far corner, something straight out of the 90s. “I just kind of hit it,” Bellingham reckoned; not wanting to hit it too hard, it had gone “looping”, “stabbing”, he said. “Normally [my goals are] a lot closer, aren’t they? I was a bit surprised, honestly. Normally from there I’m looking to see who is an option to play it through to, but it popped up nicely. It was nice.” Nice? It was, Silva said, “special”. A “work of art” Marca called it. The presenter on one radio station claimed it was the best goal he had ever seen, and it wasn’t just him; wasn’t just the goal, either. Continue reading...

articles.author: Osasu Obayiuwana in Lagos
articles.content: After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history. As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday , was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute. Continue reading...

articles.author: Tom Service
articles.content: Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprises of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill. Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang . And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she could have come up with. Continue reading...

articles.content: Caitlin brings her ultimate comfort food to the table: a celebration of carbs and dairy. From teenage music journalist to bestselling feminist author, Caitlin Moran has spent her life asking questions, challenging convention and making us laugh along the way. She's interviewed rock stars, changed the conversation around feminism and written some of the funniest observations about modern life. She reveals what it was like growing up as the eldest of eight children in a home-schooled, unconventional family, learning to cook from library books. She also looks back on her teenage years as a music journalist, touring with the likes of Radiohead and the Beastie Boys, her early experiences of fame and the making of How to Be a Woman. Plus, she opens up about her relationship with food and body image, and how she came to recognise and eventually let go of the anxiety she once thought was essential to her creativity. New episodes of Comfort Eating with Siobhán are out every Wednesday. Continue reading...

articles.content: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sadiq Khan
articles.content: Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree. Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most. Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.author: Phil Hoad
articles.content: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024). Continue reading...

articles.author: Florence Hallett
articles.content: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church. Continue reading...

A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church. articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.content: Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs. As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes . It’s a common issue. Continue reading...

articles.content: Ahead of him rounding out the year at a huge London show, the DJ legend will join us to answer your questions Beatifically smiling as he sends another packed dancefloor into raptures, Carl Cox is one of the most enduring and reliably euphoria-inducing figures in UK club culture history. As he prepares to close out the current season at Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, and looks towards a return of his residency at Ibiza nightclub Unvrs, he will join us to answer your questions. Known for playing a banging yet nuanced blend of house and techno, Cox’s career stretches back to the age of 10, learning his craft growing up in London and later Brighton, funding nights out by trimming his neighbours’ hedges. As Chicago house, Detroit techno and other new styles hit the UK, Cox was primed to receive them: fluidly mixing across three decks at once, he immersed himself in both the illegal rave scene and the new wave of nightclubs cropping up to showcase this music. Continue reading...

articles.content: Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.content: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

articles.author: Sali Hughes
articles.content: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. If this sounds like a kids’ party from hell, blame me, because it’s actually perfectly pleasant, got me heaps of compliments and got better and mellower as the hours passed. If you’re a milk with three sugars sort of a person, I think you may love it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Peter Bradshaw
articles.content: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . Continue reading...

articles.content: Controlled blast to proceed after multiple delays and outpouring of concern about potential health and environmental effects The US Army is set to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, moving ahead after multiple delays and despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. The controlled blast is planned to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemicals stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes. Continue reading...

It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. Continue reading...

articles.content: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. Continue reading...

articles.content: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Continue reading...

articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.content: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart. More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare? Continue reading...

articles.content: Plus: the quickest team to go from FA Cup winners to the first round and matches delayed by snowball fights Mail us with all of your questions and answers “Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. articles.content: Apple’s tone-deaf Karate Kid knock-off feels like a Maga-approved after-school special It’s hard to avoid the reports that boys and young men are in trouble . Across the US and UK, they’re outpaced by girls on reading tests, are more likely to have behavioral difficulties and exposed to impossible body image standards by the manosphere. You might think that all of this would make you think extra carefully about a film that centers on a 13-year-old boy. Not in the case of Way of the Warrior Kid, a cliche-ridden celebration of machismo and the military that greets the current climate with a shrug. At times, I had to remind myself that I wasn’t watching a Maga-funded after-school special. Continue reading...

articles.author: Cath Clarke
articles.content: Tenderly drawn story combines a history of surfing with an emotional account of losing a partner to bone cancer aged 24 This gently moving and beautifully animated drama is adapted from an award-winning graphic novel by Californian illustrator AJ Dungo . His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe. AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them. Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the sea and surfing here, and a gentle tapping into surfing’s spiritual side; a handful of gorgeous scenes in a palette of mushroom brown and grey tell snippets of its origins in Polynesia. At heart, In Waves is an idealistic, emotional film, handling its subject delicately, avoiding too much of the rawness of grief. I can imagine older kids and teenagers falling deeply in love with it. Continue reading...

articles.author: George Monbiot
articles.content: Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead . Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure” , and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jennifer Walker
articles.content: A neighbourhood that transforms into a living advent calendar, hot chocolate beneath chandeliers and 16th-century baths – Hungary’s capital is full of winter warmth Each December, my neighbourhood on the Buda side of the Danube transforms into a living advent calendar. On the edge of District XI (Újbuda), the 1930s OTI estate in Albertfalva is known for its rustic looking single-storey houses with rounded doorways and green shutters. From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. For something grander, I’ll cross the Danube into Pest for its Christmas markets and elaborately decorated shop fronts. Last November, my friends and I sipped hot chocolate beneath the crystal chandeliers of the Művész Kávéház , a historic cafe on Andrássy út, waiting for the Christmas lights to be switched on outside, illuminating the boulevard and the Hungarian State Opera House. Continue reading...

articles.author: Mythili Rao
articles.content: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather. Continue reading...

articles.content: With my career stalled and my dreams unfulfilled, I was starting to write myself off. But my ideas about ageing were all wrong … It was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me. When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back of my right arm. Continue reading...

articles.content: The Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later director is preparing to launch his biopic of Rupert Murdoch’s early years as a British tabloid mogul. In anticipation of its New Year release, the director will be taking your questions You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting. Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it. Instead he went into theatre, became deputy director of the Royal Court, then swerved into television, directing Inspector Morse among other things. His first film, Shallow Grave, arrived in 1994; two years later Trainspotting tore British cinema a new one. In 2009, Slumdog Millionaire won him the best director Oscar. He also masterminded the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, somehow squeezing industrial chimneys, NHS beds, James Bond, Mr Bean and the history of British pop into one stadium. Continue reading...

articles.content: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” Continue reading...

articles.author: Flora Willson
articles.content: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. Thirteen years since winning the coveted Pulitzer for Partita for 8 Voices – an exhilarating unaccompanied vocal work that mixes speech and singing, baroque dances and analogue versions of studio-mixed effects – Shaw has a CV like no other. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jonathan Liew
articles.content: Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television? Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis. Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian Continue reading...

articles.content: The battle over the Matthew and Hunter islands – and their 350,000 sq km economic zone – has made its way to the UN’s highest court Two tiny specks of volcanic land in the vast Pacific Ocean – home to seabirds and not much else – are at the centre of an escalating territorial battle between France and Vanuatu. The decades-long dispute over the Matthew and Hunter islands has entered a new phase, with Vanuatu launching two separate international legal proceedings against France as part of its attempt to claim these Pacific territories. Arbitration proceedings began last month, which could threaten France’s claim to a vast expanse of the ocean surrounding the islands. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andy Burnham
articles.content: The NDAs that enforce silence, the behaviour that exploits the age of consent. I'll address both with sweeping changes to keep women and girls safe Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation. Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. Sadly, many women and girls will find the recent stories all too close to home, whether it’s casual disrespect in the workplace, undermining “jokes”, or being told they are somehow at fault for something that has happened to them. Continue reading...

articles.content: Former Bake Off colleagues Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig revisit the former’s home in a travelogue where they’re having the best time – as is everyone watching Sandi Toksvig is one of TV’s great pootlers. There are few sights as cheering as that of the tiny Dane, bundled up in a scarf, bimbling along a coastal path, or scurrying down a continental alleyway, like a Womble that’s just been chased out of a boulangerie after a misunderstanding over a bun. Said perambulations are generally accompanied by an accessory of some sort, an unofficial mascot for each of her pootle-based travelogues. In Sandi’s Great Riviera Rail Trip, for instance, it was a small suitcase. In Extraordinary Escapes With Sandi Toksvig it was Britain’s orangest cagoule. Now, in Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure, it’s Prue Leith. Continue reading...

articles.author: Nick Ames at the Etihad Stadium
articles.content: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons at Emirates Stadium
articles.content: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. Continue reading...

articles.content: Victory expands Democrats’ House majority, its largest advantage in three decades Democrat Victoria Broderick has won Tennessee’s fourth congressional district, unseating eight-term Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais in one of the biggest House upsets of the cycle. The victory expands Democrats’ historic House majority in the 120th Congress to 259 seats, the party’s largest advantage in three decades , and flips a seat that Donald Trump carried by more than 20 points in 2024. Broderick, 34, a former technology and logistics professional who previously ran for Congress in 2024, told the Guardian in an interview before her race was called that she connected with constituents who had not voted in years and met Republicans concerned about affordability who appreciated the “integrity” she brought to the race. Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it . Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK. Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. articles.content: Shabana Mahmood’s ‘new impartiality standard’ for police is not non-political, argues Chris Sinha . Plus a letter from Dr Peter Purton The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, says police in uniform should not participate in LGBTQ+ pride events, saying that “at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act” ( Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform, 18 November ). She also said that it is wrong for the police not to be colour-blind in policing, as in the previous anti-racism commitment – a commitment that reflected the recognition of the history of systemic racism, and of the perceptions of the police by communities who are policed – and that the police should not engage with “activist groups and campaigners”. Instead, they should adhere to “a new impartiality standard”. Continue reading...

articles.content: The former Labour prime minister is wrong to dismiss all zero-sum thinking as misguided, writes Gavin Bailey The broad thrust of Gordon Brown’s argument is correct ( The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same, 22 November ). However, he is wrong to suggest that zero-sum beliefs are erroneous. Many things in life are zero-sum. If I own a house, you can’t also own it; if I burn some gas to heat it, you can’t use the same gas. If the UK makes all the cars for the European market, other countries’ carmakers won’t be making them. Yes, growth can come from collaboration and trade, but the proceeds are not infinite and take time to achieve. Continue reading...

If the UK makes all the cars for the European market, other countries’ carmakers won’t be making them. Yes, growth can come from collaboration and trade, but the proceeds are not infinite and take time to achieve. Continue reading...
articles.title: Gordon Brown’s ideas on zero-sum beliefs don’t add up | Letters

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.content: The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses ( Letters, 15 November ), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence. Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles. Continue reading...

articles.content: Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself. Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. articles.author: Natalie Morris
articles.content: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.content: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous. Continue reading...

articles.content: Eminent Shakespeare scholar and author who brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works. Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial. Continue reading...

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.content: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. Continue reading...

articles.content: After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time. But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Alice Fisher
articles.content: A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised? Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. Continue reading...

articles.content: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Geoffrey Robertson
articles.content: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.content: Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature. John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under. Continue reading...

articles.content: When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit . It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did. Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4. Continue reading...

articles.author: Charlotte Jansen
articles.content: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something. Continue reading...

articles.content: Viewing figures are up and the new judge has spiced up the show with her wit, charm and articulate appreciation of doughy delights. Prompting a public outpouring of love, magisterial Lawson has proved the missing ingredient in the show’s resurgence. Continue reading...

articles.content: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.content: Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party? Dan, by email We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals . The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all associate with the festive season”. If there’s a gang coming over, you’ll likely find Pink ladling hot mulled apple juice laced with citrussy gin into mugs, or making pitchers of rum punch: “Either would warm the cockles.” Alternatively, consider a “slightly lighter” mulled white wine: “Gently warm your favourite white wine with spices such as star anise, cinnamon, ginger and cloves, sweeten with syrup and citrus, then spike with apple cider brandy.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue reading...

articles.content: Royal Albert Hall, London The Royal Philharmonic rode the bucking rhythms of the star composer’s intricate score, the highlight of an evening that also included works by Steve Reich and David Lang If anyone tells you that classical music is dead you need just two words to refute them: Joe Hisaishi. articles.content: The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF). “Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.” ‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest Continue reading...
