articles.content: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London? Continue reading...

History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London? Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch

articles.content: Plus five fantastic recipes, from seared tuna and potato to spicy butternut and lentil, to show how it’s done Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls. The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to balance it with ingredients that offset its soporific qualities. It’s a good stress test for our guidelines, in fact: if you can turn a root-and-grain combination into a bright and balanced salad, you’re on to a winner. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
articles.content: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jane Hoskyn
articles.content: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites • The best beauty Advent calendars • The best Christmas baubles In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025. Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades. Continue reading...

articles.content: It will help during winter months, but there are better solutions for really thirsty plants The problem With the onset of winter, the heating comes on, humidity drops and tropical plants that yearn for rainforest conditions end up in something closer to a desert. Cue crispy leaf edges. Humidifiers work, but they require buying, filling and cleaning. Misting works, but you need to remember to do it. So, a free, lazy alternative has an obvious appeal. The hack This hack is based on transpiration. Plants constantly release water vapour through their leaves, so huddling them together raises the humidity around them. Continue reading...

articles.author: Leslie Felperin
articles.content: A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at first. Although Gara calls Nada her daughter, the young girl is actually her niece; Gara adopted her after her sister, Nada’s mum, was killed by a violent husband. Gara’s profound grief and loss haunt her every day, felt most painfully, perhaps, when an animal dies on the heath, reminding them of the fragility of life. Continue reading...

articles.author: Peter Bradshaw
articles.content: Yoon Ga-eun’s film tracks the uneasy fallout after a teenage schoolgirl makes a deeply shocking announcement to her class Korean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke. Continue reading...

articles.author: Oliver Bullough
articles.content: A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. Continue reading...

articles.author: Fergal Kinney
articles.content: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. Continue reading...

articles.author: Angela Giuffrida
articles.content: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo . Continue reading...

articles.author: Rich Pelley
articles.content: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the roof. At least, I assume it was a pet. I can’t think of any other reason that doesn’t sound considerably more sinister. Continue reading...

articles.author: Beejay Silcox
articles.content: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
articles.content: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground. There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. articles.content: The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him How did you get into comedy? I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy. Who did you admire when you were starting out? It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney. Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London , on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May Continue reading...

articles.author: Nadia Khomami
articles.content: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.author: Erica Jeal
articles.content: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. Mullov-Abbado’s violin writing is as gratifying as you’d hope for from the son of Viktoria Mullova , and his jazz-classical fusion hits an unusually effective sweet spot. Continue reading...

articles.author: Annilese Miskimmon
articles.content: The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . Continue reading...

I noticed that she wasn’t wearing a collar. I thought to myself, that dog clearly doesn’t belong there – she needs help. Why is she out on her own? Workers at the construction site had built her a small shack, complete with a water bowl and food dish. Although she was spending some time there, whenever they would get too close she would run off. Continue reading...

articles.content: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Paul Sullivan
articles.content: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. Continue reading...

articles.author: Simon Hattenstone
articles.content: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.author: Philip Oltermann
articles.content: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog . The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with collaborators. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sophie Williams
articles.content: Utilita Arena Cardiff Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. Continue reading...

articles.author: Gaby Hinsliff
articles.content: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. ( Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than quadrupled after an episode of Clarkson’s Farm in which Jeremy Clarkson’s partner, Lisa Hogan, persuaded him to grow them to make supplements, claiming that “everyone who’s anyone” is on them.) Continue reading...

articles.content: The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle. Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats, and one of my seasonal highlights is spotting couples or whole families engaged in furious arguments while wearing reindeer antlers or giant turkeys on their heads. Continue reading...

articles.content: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. Continue reading...

articles.author: Priya Elan
articles.content: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. Elsewhere, Tate McRae recently wore a black sequined butterfly bra and matching butterfly wing belt from lingerie wunderkind Ludovic de Saint Sernin. Both Swedish popstar Zara Larsson and her fans are championing glittery butterfly makeup motifs. Continue reading...

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.content: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. Continue reading...
